body: On November 22, 2025, thirteen of us travelling with Flamingo Lanka visited the revered Abhayagiri stupa. It is one of the most significant and monumental landmarks in the ancient capitol Anuradhapura.Abhyagiri was once a thriving center of Buddhist learning and monastic life. Established in the 1st century BC by King Walagamba, it grew into a renowned international institution, attracting scholars from distant lands. The Chinese monk, Faxian, who visited in the 5th century recorded that the complex housed 5000 monks.The main attraction today is the Abhayagiri Stupa, standing 75 metres tall with a circumference of 350 metres. Over the centuries, the stupa had been renovated and restored maintaining its grandeur and spiritual significanceAbhayagiri remains a deeply sacred site for Buddhists and a powerful symbol of faith. Following tradition, we walked clockwise around the stupa. Buddhists among us, joined the crowds offering flowers and chanting pirith - Buddhist stanzas - venerating Buddha and his teachings creating a serene, peaceful and a tranquil atmosphere.
title: Symbol of Buddhist Faith

body: There’s some scaffolding on parts of this dagoba at the moment, so you’ll need to find the best vantage point from which to photograph it. The park as a whole is a sprawling complex with ticket checkpoints all over the place. By far the best way to see it all is on a bicycle. We spent an awesome day riding through some beautiful scenery, with monuments peeking through the foliage. Having done Polunnaruwa earlier in our trip, we found Anaradhapura a little disappointing. If you’re planning your itinerary and are unsure if you need a night or two here, I don’t think you do if you’re taking in the far superior park at Polunnaruwa. It’s all a bit same-same here. The two big dagobas are certainly impressive but the rest of the sites aren’t much to write home about. The “sacred bodhi tree” was a let down. Really just a temple for locals. You see very little of the tree itself. All in all, a lovely day out cycling through rural Sri Lanka, but the day will not be remembered for the monuments.

Dating back to 380AD, the archaeological park contains ancient ruins, dagobas and temples, and a museum.You will need to organise transport to explore it as I think there is simply too much distance to cover by foot. We opt for a tuk tuk. Others for a bicycle, that doesn't seem a bad alternative.In my opinion, in general, the whole site is pretty disappointing. As the country has better attractions (i.e.Polonnaruwa), I would visit Anuradhapura only in case you have some spare time (and an extra budget).Unfortunately, not worth it from my point of view. USEFUL INFOEntry ticket to the site: 25,00 USD per person (only cash)Journey time from Sigiriya by tuk tuk: around 1h30minsPRO TIPSince it is a religious site still in use today, please bear in mind that everybody is asked to dress properly (shoulders and knees must be covered, and shoes and hats must be removed).Because of the latter, I highly suggest to carry also a pair of socks into your bag as sometimes the ground can be very warm/hot.

body: The Abhayagiri Dagoba is a huge brick stupa built slightly over 2,000 years ago, and for centuries after that, served as the focal point of an expansive monastery complex, stretching for hectares around. Other than sheer size, the stupa itself isn’t much to see -- though you should spend some time contemplating its age and the feat of construction it represented for its time -- but the parkland around is chockful of ruined foundations of all sorts of buildings.The stupa/dagoba was the focal centre of a major monastic complex, said to once have housed and served 5,000 monks. Today, it’s a shady area with mature trees, with hardly anyone else around, so it’s a pleasant stroll wandering around the ruins. As bonus, I saw three wild peacocks strutting around the site too.Not so pleasant were inquisitive monkeys and wild dogs.Also, sun block cream and insect repellent would be handy.Among the ruins to the east, a short walk away leads you to a lovely piece of sculpture called the Samadhi Buddha. More ruins can be found to the west of the stupa; these ruins (“Ratnaprasada”) once housed the more ascetic monks. To the northwest of the stupa is the most elaborately-carved “moonstone” in Anuradhapura -- a “moonstone” is a stone slab placed before a set of steps.It’s interesting to try to imagine the hustle and bustle that once characterised this site, with monks chanting prayers, debating sacred texts, and lay people presenting donations. No doubt it was also a location for political intrigue since organised religion was closely intertwined with government in those times. I also wondered what sort of economy could support such a large number of monks.But today, it’s a tranquil, relaxing parkland.About 300 – 400m south of Abhayagiri Dagoba is the Abhayagiri Museum. See my review of it under that name.The stupa, museum and ruins around are all within the paid area of Anuradhapura's “Sacred City/Ancient Ruins” archaeological park. However, tickets to the Archaeological park can only be purchased from the Archaeological Museum (not to be confused with the Abhayagiri Museum) located about 2 km south (ridiculous!) of the Abhayagiri Dagoba. Cost = US$25, or 3,780 Sri Lankan rupees and valid only for the same day.General info about places in the “Sacred City/Ancient Ruins” park: The sights are quite spread out such that while walking from one sight to the second may be possible, covering many more on foot is impractical. You’ll need a map and a bicycle or tuktuk hired for the day. Also, there few toilets, and few places to buy water, though there is at least one rustic shop near the Abhayagiri Dagoba that has cold drinking water for sale.
title: Don't just visit the stupa, wander about the nearby ruins too

body: When you set aside religion and look at these ancient sights as landmarks to this area and to the country. As a tourist they are worth a visit as much as you would visit the Eiffel Tower in Paris and the Statue of Liberty in New York etc, etc.There is something to get from visiting them. Something to feel and understand. It is the feeling of the heat of the paved slabs or rock steps under your feet and an appreciation and understanding forming of what worship is like for these people here. It is the physical exertion on your body to reach the highest point. It is the tranquility of the landscape that these sights are built around. It is the bewilderment of the age of the relics and the size in which some have been made. It is the sights of monkeys behaving like this is their home. It is the noise of traditional music as an organ may be playing if you were to visit a Cathedral. It is the gentle murmurs of worship coming from peoples prayers. It is the shade of the tree whether it be regarded as holy or not. It is the smell of incense and the sight of flowers given as a gift. It is the welcoming smiles of the Sri Lankan people who are happy to include you here regardless of your religion.It is something you do and recommend you do when you are visiting another country.
title: It's A Landmark Thing And As A Tourist ...

It once stood an imposing 115 meters tall but part of the pinnaccle fell off and it is some 30 m lower. The pinnacle can be seen behind the dogoba, lying on the ground.You enter thru 2 large white stupas affairs then in front of the dagoba is an image house with a large highly painted reclining buddha in it. The walls of the image house are highly decorated too. As you walk around the Dagoba -there are a number of statues and on the cardinal points there are highly carved stone structures.

body: Abhayagiriya Stupa is a part of a major monastery (Abhayagiriya Monastery) in Sri Lanka in ancient times. It has been built around 80 BC by King Valagamba. Abhayagiriya monastery was spread over a large area. Today also the remains can be seen in a large area around the Abhayagiriya Stupa. If you visit this place, make sure to visit them also. 'Vahalkada' is also an important feature of this stupa. Two of them are remaining and they are conservated. And also fine stone carvings can be seen here. Finer stone carvings can be seen in other remains around the stupa, such as 'Moonstone' and 'Guard stones'. I would recommend this place as a must visit place is Anuradhapura. Further, parking spaces are available at Abhayagiri Stupa.

body: This is the 2nd oldest of the Great monasteries in Anuradhapura where about 5000 monks lived during the Anuradhapura kingdom. The surrounding remains of the monastery which is impressive and covered by grass. This gives you are nice view and easy access. This is the smaller one of 2 brick stone dagobas in Anuradhapura but it is the third of Anuradhapura's great stupas which was one of the creative work by king walagamba. It is one of the sacred sites and definitely worth the trip. If you have time on your tour, this is a good place for a rest in the park areas surrounding the ruins. Bicycles are the best way to get around. They can be hired for around LKR 450. King Walagamaba built it by demolishing a place occupied by "giri" who insulted him on his defeat on the war. The size and complexity of the sacred city is amazing. This was a complex that comprises of many buildings, statutes and ponds . Only the ruins can be seen today.There is a lot of nice green location around for photo lovers. The scale of the dome is what makes this place unique . A must visit in Anuradhapura. We went on a really hot day and could hardly walk without shoes on the stone floor as we have to remove shoes as it is a place of worship with shrine rooms. Please bring socks. It is a huge stupa and was the 2nd biggest building in the world when made. Visually stunning. This colossal stupa soars above the forest floor. It is constructed of bricks, its scale is matched only by the Giza pyramids from what I heard about. The dagoba itself is interesting, but the area around it is well worth exploring. There are so many ruins that were fun to walk around to find special elements that made some of them unique. Riding a bicycle is the perfect way to be able to explore this area. Remember to stop and walk around for a close up experience. This is the most popular place among Sri Lankan people. Abayagiri dagoba is a very beautiful place. I found it very peaceful, a lot more majestic than the other stupas. The difference in colour from the normal white stupas makes it very beautiful. I recommend you to visit it during evenings to go here. Leave early, as it takes over 3 hours to get around, and the middle of the day is too hot.

body: ABHAYAGIRI TEMPLEAbhayagiri Vihara (temple) in Anuradhapura is one of the most sacred places and oldest temples of Theravada Buddhism. It is one of eight most venerated places (Atamasthana) and one of the five highest/tallest Viharas in Anuradhapura. Abhayagiri monastery was founded by King Vatttagamani Abhaya (also called Valagambahu) (89-77 BC) in 88 BC.as a religious school. Originally its height was more than 330 feet and it was built on the ruins of a Jain hermitage, destroyed by Abhaya. Within next 200 years it became a great international institution for Buddhist learning alongwith its rival orthodox monasteries of Mahavihara and Jetavana which professed Mahayana Buddhism. Abhayagiri means ‘Hill of Protection’ or ‘Fearless Hill’. Reportedly a statue of a bull made of pure gold, containing relics of the Buddha was buried in the core of the stupa. Reportedly the dagoba was built over a footprint of the Buddha with a circumference of 1300 feet (400 meters).
title: Magnificent Ancient Vihara

body: Abhayagiri Vihāra was a major monastery site of Mahayana and Theravada Buddhism that was situated in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka. It is one of the most extensive ruins in the world and one of the most sacred Buddhist pilgrimage cities in the nation. Historically it was a great monastic centre as well as a royal capital, with magnificent monasteries rising to many stories, roofed with gilt bronze or tiles of burnt clay glazed in brilliant colors. To the north of the city, encircled by great walls and containing elaborate bathing ponds, carved balustrades and moonstones, stood "Abhayagiri", one of seventeen such religious units in Anuradhapura and the largest of its five major viharas. One of the focal points of the complex is an ancient stupa, the Abhayagiri Dagaba. Surrounding the humped dagaba, Abhayagiri Vihara was a seat of the Northern Monastery, or Uttara Vihara.

body: Whether the LKR3.5K/foreigner fee (half price for under-13s) for access to Anuradhapura’s ruins is “worth it” depends on your expectations. Angkor Wat it’s not; but it’s cool. If you want to see it, pay it (and if you don’t, don’t). (Sure, you can sneak around and see most stuff without having paid. But do you think of yourself as a cheater? If not, why cheat?) NB at least as of the date of this review, the Archeology Museum is “closed for renovations.” That sucks. But, expectations. The guards didn’t seem to like us climbing up the base rings of the Abhayagiri Dagoba (stupa). That sucks. But, expectations. The Sanctuary at Tissawewa, which we’d pegged to be high-class, was a disappointment. No ice! No Diet Coke! “No, we don’t have that dish, or that one either.” The “New Zealand beef” in the salad was practically inedible. Expectations. The contemporary-Buddhism-related sites (temples, the tree) require legs be covered down to below the knee. Dress appropriately, or buy and carry a sarong to put over your shorts (or borrow one from your guesthouse host). Par contre, the “wear white” signs didn’t seem enforced at all. The tree, although it certainly didn’t look 2,300 years old (and probably is a descendant of the original tree, not actually it), felt like the most genuine piece of Anuradhapura. The bikes our guesthouse gave us, like all the other bikes we saw tourists on, were complete crap, which measurably decreased the pleasure of cycling around. On our way out of town we noticed a sign for Indika Bikes, at the Tourist Information Center Restaurant between the Dutugemunu Roundabout and The Lakeside at Nuwarawewa (across from the tyre place) looked like it was offering nicer bikes.
title: Expectations

body: Let me first preface by saying Anuradhapura is a long distance to travel from the main coastal resorts and so you should probably only consider if you are touring the island. It was about a two hour drive from Sigiriya. The area is too big to cover on foot in a single day and, whilst bicycles and TukTuks are easy and cheap to hire, I would recommend a driver/guide who can direct you to and provide commentary on the most significant sites. Abhayaagiri was a complex of monastic buildings founded in the first or second century BC. It is still being uncovered and restored. The stupa is huge (230fit high and very similar to Jethavanarama) but as it still under renovation there is lots of scaffolding. The grounds are the main attraction. The Twin Bathing Pools (Kottum Putan) are very tranquil and worth a 5-10 minute stop as it’s a great example of the amazing engineering and water management that was typical across ancient Sri Lanka. Here solid stone was carved out to create two large pools used by thousands of monks for bathing. Elsewhere across the island earth was excavated on an even larger scale to create huge water tanks which were used for feeding crops as well as bathing. If you are in the area I would recommend that you also visit the ruins of King Mahasen’s Palace to see an exquisite example of a moonstone doorstep with finely detailed symbolic carvings; the Ratnaprasada (Gem Place) for the guardstone; and the Mahapali Refectory with its huge rice trough and bathing pools.
title: Exquiste moonstone and guardstone - best in the area

body: While the stupa is monumental, one of the best parts of Anuradapura was wandering in the very extensive area covered by these ancient monastery ruins, still not widely recovered and restored from the overgrowth. Check out the big pools as well and have a good wander around the fallen down monastery residences that stretch out through the woods.

body: It was a complex of monastic buildings founded in 2nd century BC. The Abhayagiri Dagaba was built by King Valagamba between 89-77 BC. Periodic South Indian invasions led to the disintegration of the Abhayagiri Vihara. When it was rediscovered in the 1880s, it was a lost city - over grown with trees and the dagoba was reduced to a mountain of bricks. The brick foundation runs horizontally as tall as the Dagoba. At the moment, renovations are underway with the help of the Central Cultural Found and volunteers who flock to help cut a trench, carry a brick, lay a stone at the ancient Vihara. Expected completion of renovations is Dec 2012.
